## Frequently asked questions
### Is prop money legal to buy and use in Australia?
Yes. Prop currency is completely legal to purchase and use in Australia for legitimate motion picture, television, theatrical, commercial, and training productions provided it adheres to the Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 and Reserve Bank of Australia reproduction guidelines, featuring prominent non-negotiable reproduction markings.

### Can this prop money be spent or circulated as legal tender?
Absolutely not. PROPPS PTY LTD reproduction currency is strictly non-legal tender. Attempting to spend, circulate, or deceive any person or machine with prop currency is a severe criminal offence under Commonwealth law carrying substantial prison penalties.

### What materials are used for your Australian prop banknotes?
Our prop currency is printed on specialized 120gsm high-grade matte archival paper rather than polymer film. This matte finish prevents studio camera reflections, handles realistically during counting scenes, and ensures clear distinction from genuine legal currency.

### What is the minimum order requirement and shipping cost?
Our minimum order value is $150 AUD. Orders of $500 AUD and above qualify for free Australia-wide express shipping. Orders below $500 incur a flat $20 AUD Australia Post Express shipping fee with mandatory signature on delivery.

### How does the 10% cryptocurrency discount work?
When selecting cryptocurrency payment (Bitcoin, USDT TRC20, or Ethereum), a 10% discount is automatically deducted from your order subtotal. You will receive transfer instructions and can confirm your transaction with a TXID.

### Do you offer bulk wholesale pricing for film production studios?
Yes. We supply major streaming studios, theatre companies, escape rooms, and financial training institutions across Australia with custom bulk quantities, specialised serial numbers, and custom vault bricks with tiered wholesale discounts.

### Where are you based and how fast is dispatch?
We are based in Melbourne, Victoria (Eltham, VIC 3093). All orders are packaged discreetly in tamper-evident security boxes and dispatched via Express Australia Post within 24 business hours of payment confirmation.

### How much does prop money cost?
Orders start at $150 AUD. Published bundles run from a Starter Stack ($1,500 face value, $115) up to 100 Stacks ($200,000 face value, $14,000). Cryptocurrency payments get 10% off, and studio quantities can ask about wholesale tiers of 10% to 30% off.

### Does prop money feel like real money?
Our notes are printed double-sided on matte archival paper, so they read as money on camera but feel like paper, not polymer, in the hand. That difference, plus the specimen marking, keeps them clearly props.

### Can you take prop money on a plane in Australia?
Generally yes on domestic flights when the notes are clearly marked, packed as strapped stacks and carried with the supplier invoice. International travel needs customs checks at both ends. Check the airline rules before you fly.

## Guides
### Play Money Kmart Australia: Kmart Play Money vs a Prop Money Supplier
- URL: https://aupropmoney.com/blog/play-money-kmart-vs-a-prop-money-supplier-what-to-buy-in-australia/
- Published: 2026-11-28

Search for play money Kmart and you will find people asking the same question from two angles. Some want a cheap box of toy notes for a kids' shop game this weekend. Others have already tried the toy aisle, found the notes too small, too flimsy or not very Australian, and want to know where to buy something better. This guide compares Kmart play money, which is the typical big-box toy product, with buying from a prop money supplier. It is general information, not a recommendation to avoid any retailer, and the range in any store changes, so check what is on the shelf or online before you go.

## The short answer

If you need a small amount of colourful play money for young children and you are happy with a basic toy, the toy aisle at a department store is the fast, low-cost option. If you need Australian-style notes, a larger quantity, sturdier paper or notes for a classroom, party, photo or film, a prop money supplier is the better fit. Either way, the notes should be clearly play or prop money, never anything that could be passed as real. [Shop our Australian play money](/shop/event-and-party-props/) if you want ready-made sets.

## Why people search for Kmart play money

Kmart, Big W, Target and Officeworks are where Australians go for toys, craft and school supplies, so a search that starts with a store name is usually someone who wants it now and wants it cheap. The same searcher often adds words such as fake money Kmart, play money notes or kids play money. That is a buyer with a clear need, which is why the answer should be practical rather than a lecture.

## Kmart play money: what to expect

Toy-aisle play money is built for young children playing shop or board games. In general you can expect a few things, although you should check the current product because lines change.

- Bright, cartoon-style notes that are obviously not real currency.

- A small number of notes in a single pack, often a mixed set of denominations or coins.

- Light paper or card that suits a few games but tears with heavy use.

- Low cost per pack, which is the main reason people buy it.

- Designs that may not match Australian notes, so older children and teachers who want to practise real amounts may find it limiting.

None of that is a criticism. It is the right product for a toddler's toy shop. It is just a different product from a prop supplier's notes.

## Prop money supplier notes: what to expect

A prop money supplier sells notes made for a purpose: a class, an event, a photo or a film. For Australian buyers that usually means notes in the familiar $5, $10, $20, $50 and $100 sizes and colours, printed on proper paper and carrying a clear non-legal-tender marking. PROPPS notes carry specimen markings so they read as props, not as currency. They are sold in stacks, so you can buy what the job needs rather than a toy-sized handful. See our guide on [what to check when buying Australian play money](/blog/australian-play-money-where-to-buy-and-what-to-check/).

## Kmart play money vs prop supplier: side by side

| Question | Toy-aisle play money | Prop money supplier |
|---|---|---|
| Best for | Young children, a one-off game | Classrooms, parties, photos, film |
| Look | Cartoon or generic | Australian denominations and colours |
| Quantity | One small pack | Stacks and bulk packs |
| Paper | Light, short life | Heavier, built for handling |
| Markings | Play money text | Specimen or non-legal-tender marking |
| Delivery | Pick up in store or order online | Express Post with signature |

## Which should you buy?

For a kids' shop game or a birthday present: the toy aisle is fine. Keep the notes in a box, count them back in and enjoy it.

For a classroom: teachers need the Australian denominations and enough notes for a whole class. Our guide to [fake money for classroom lessons by year level](/blog/fake-money-for-classroom-play-money-lessons-by-year-level/) explains the numbers.

For a party, casino night or photo booth: you want notes that look good in a photo and that guests can toss about. The [event and party prop cash pack](/shop/event-and-party-props/event-and-party-prop-cash-pack/) is made for that, and our guide to [fake money for parties](/blog/fake-money-for-parties-casino-nights-birthdays-weddings/) has set-ups.

For a film, a music video or a shoot: buy proper prop notes in stacks, not toys. Read [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/).

## A note on fake money Kmart searches

Searches for fake money Kmart are almost always about toy notes for games and parties. They are not a reason to use anything that looks like real money. Whatever you buy, the legal line is the same: play and prop notes are fine when they are clearly marked as props and used as props. They must never be spent, passed on or used to mislead anyone. The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) covers counterfeit currency, and the [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions. Our [compliance page](/compliance/) explains how PROPPS builds to that standard, and the guide to [fake money vs prop money in Australia](/blog/fake-money-vs-prop-money-the-legal-difference-in-australia/) covers the difference in plain language.

## What to check before you buy any play money

1. Does it say play or specimen on every note? It should be obvious at a glance.

2. Is it the right size and denomination for the age group? Younger children need big, simple notes; older children benefit from real Australian values.

3. How many do you need? Count the users, then add a spare set. Running out mid-game ruins the activity.

4. How tough is the paper? If the notes will be handled daily, buy heavier stock.

5. Who is the seller? An Australian supplier that issues an invoice and ships with tracking is easier to deal with if something is wrong. The [ACCC](https://www.accc.gov.au/) explains your consumer guarantees.

## How many notes do you need?

As a guide, a pair of children playing shop needs one mixed set. A class of 24 sharing in groups of four needs six sets plus a teacher's bank. A party of 30 playing a casino game needs a float for each guest. The easiest way to avoid a shortage is to buy slightly more than the headcount suggests. Notes that are not used can be stored flat for next time.

## Common mistakes with play money

- Buying one small pack for a whole group. Splitting a tiny set between several children ends in arguments.

- Choosing realistic notes for a loose party. Lots of guests, lots of pockets: use clearly pretend notes.

- Using play money as a joke payment. Never. It can cause real trouble for you and for staff.

- Forgetting storage. A zip bag or box keeps the set together for next time.

- Ignoring delivery time. If the party is on Saturday, order early in the week. See the [shipping policy](/shipping-policy/).

## Where PROPPS fits

PROPPS is a Melbourne supplier of non-legal-tender prop currency. We sell Australian-style notes in stacks, a kit for party cash cannons and bulk packs for productions. If you are choosing between a toy-aisle pack and something sturdier, start with the [event and party prop cash pack](/shop/event-and-party-props/event-and-party-prop-cash-pack/) and the full [play money range](/shop/event-and-party-props/). If you are not sure which suits your job, [contact the studio](/contact/) with the date and quantity.

## A quick shopping checklist
Before you spend anything, write down four answers: who will use the money, how many people will use it at once, how long you need it to last and where it will be used. A child's bedroom shop needs a few dozen notes for a year. A school needs several hundred notes for a decade. A party needs a float for every guest for one night. A film needs stacks for a week. Matching the purchase to the job is the difference between a good buy and a drawer full of torn paper.

## Questions to ask in the toy aisle
Pick up the pack and check the back. How many notes are inside? Is every denomination represented, or is the pack mostly $1 notes? Does the packaging say what ages it suits? Are there coins as well as notes, and are the coins plastic or card? Is there any marking on the notes that makes clear they are play money? If the pack is sealed in plastic, check the photograph on the back, because the contents sometimes look different from the front of the box. These questions take thirty seconds and prevent the most common regret, which is discovering the pack has far fewer notes than the picture suggested.

## Questions to ask an online prop supplier
Online, the questions are different. Is the seller based in Australia? Is there a clear delivery estimate? Does the listing say the notes are non-legal-tender props, and is there a compliance page you can read? Will you receive a tax invoice? What is the refund policy? How is the order shipped, and do you need to be home to sign for it? A reliable supplier answers all of these on its site. PROPPS publishes its [compliance page](/compliance/), [shipping policy](/shipping-policy/) and [refund policy](/refund-policy/) so you can read them before you order.

## What children actually need
Younger children need large, simple notes and plenty of low values. Older children benefit from real Australian values because the numbers match what they see in shops. Children between about five and ten gain the most from a set with enough small notes to practise giving change. A typical mistake is buying a set that is all large notes, which leaves nothing to make change with. If you are buying for a classroom, ask teachers which denominations they use most. Many choose $5, $10 and $20 notes for younger years and add $50 and $100 notes for upper primary.

## How to store play money so it lasts
Whatever you buy, storage decides how long it lasts. Use a flat box with dividers or zip bags for each denomination, keep it out of direct sunlight and away from damp, and count the notes at the start and end of every session. Label the box with the number of notes inside so you can tell at a glance if anything is missing. Children can help with the counting, which doubles as a maths exercise. If notes get creased, press them flat under a heavy book overnight.

## When a prop supplier is the clear winner
There are a few situations where the toy aisle is simply the wrong tool. If you need notes that look right in a photograph, a toy pack will look like a toy. If you are filming, a toy pack will look cheap on camera. If you need hundreds of notes, the cost per note adds up and the quantity is usually not available in one shop. If you want invoices for a school, club or business, an online supplier provides them. In these cases a prop supplier is the better fit, and our [film and TV prop currency](/shop/film-and-tv-props/) and [photography prop set](/shop/photography-props/photography-prop-currency-set/) are built for those jobs.

## When the toy aisle is enough
It is only fair to say the opposite. If your child wants a cash register toy for a birthday, buy the toy with its own notes. If you need a few notes for a family game on a rainy afternoon, the toy aisle is quick and cheap. If you are not sure whether your child will keep playing, a small pack is a sensible first step. You can always upgrade to a larger set later.

### Play Money Printouts in Australia: Print at Home or Buy a Ready-Made Set?
- URL: https://aupropmoney.com/blog/play-money-printouts-australia-print-at-home-or-buy-a-ready-made-set/
- Published: 2026-11-28

Play money printouts are one of the most searched things parents and teachers look for before a shop game, a maths lesson or a birthday. A printable sheet costs nothing, it arrives in seconds and it works for a single afternoon. Whether it is the best choice depends on how often you will use it, how many people will handle it and how much time you have. This guide compares printing at home with buying a ready-made set, with a simple way to decide. It also covers the one rule that matters: play money should be obviously play money.

## The short answer

Print play money if you need a small amount once, for a single lesson or a short game, and you have a printer and time to cut. Buy a ready-made set if you will use it more than a few times, if a group will handle it, or if you want Australian denominations that last. Ready-made notes save hours of cutting and replace themselves less often. See our [Australian play money range](/shop/event-and-party-props/) if you are leaning that way.

## What are play money printouts?

Play money printouts are sheets you print on paper or card and cut into notes. They come as free templates from school-resource and craft sites, as paid worksheets and as part of lesson packs. Designs range from simple cartoon bills to detailed copies of real currency. The first kind is exactly what you want for play. The second kind needs care, which we cover below.

## When printing is the right choice

- A one-off lesson. One class, one session, then recycle.

- A trial. You want to see if children enjoy a shop game before spending anything.

- A very small group. Two or three children, low denominations.

- A custom activity. You want to write your own values on the notes, such as points or classroom credits.

## The real cost of printing play money

Free is not the same as cheap once you add everything up.

1. Paper or card. Thin paper tears; card is better but costs more.

2. Ink. Colour printing at volume uses a lot of ink.

3. Cutting time. Cutting notes by hand for a class of 24 takes a long time.

4. Replacement. Printed notes crease, tear and go missing quickly.

5. Storage. Loose paper notes get lost between lessons.

If you are a teacher who prints notes every term, those costs repeat. A ready-made set is a one-off purchase that lasts.

## Printouts vs a ready-made set

| Factor | Printouts | Ready-made set |
|---|---|---|
| Upfront cost | Free or very low | Higher |
| Time | Print, cut, laminate | Open the box |
| Durability | Short | Long |
| Look | Varies by template | Consistent Australian notes |
| Quantity | As many as you print | Fixed per pack |
| Best for | One-off use | Repeated use |

A good compromise for classes: buy one ready-made set for the shop corner and print extra low-value notes or coupons for classroom rewards.

## The rule for any play money: keep it obviously play

This part matters more than the cost. Reproductions of Australian banknotes are regulated, and play money should never look like something that could be passed as real. The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) deals with counterfeit currency, and the [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions. Choose printouts that are clearly cartoon or play-styled, marked as play money and sized or coloured so nobody could mistake them for the real thing. If you want realistic-looking Australian notes for a photo or a film, buy marked prop notes from a supplier instead of printing your own. Our guide to [fake money vs prop money](/blog/fake-money-vs-prop-money-the-legal-difference-in-australia/) explains the difference.

## How to print play money well

If you decide to print, a few steps make the notes last.

1. Use card or heavy paper. 120 gsm or above, or laminate the notes.

2. Print each denomination on a different colour paper. It saves ink and makes sorting easy.

3. Cut with a guillotine, not scissors. Straight edges look better and handle better.

4. Number the notes in a corner. It makes counting back in easier.

5. Store by denomination. Small zip bags work well.

## Play money printouts for different jobs

Maths lessons. Low denominations, large print and plenty of $1 and $5 notes. Our [classroom guide](/blog/fake-money-for-classroom-play-money-lessons-by-year-level/) lists activities by year level.

Birthday parties and board games. A set for each player and a bank. Ready-made sets are easier because guests fight over torn notes.

Class reward systems. Print your own custom notes with the class name. Ready-made Australian notes sit alongside them for the shop.

Role play and drama. A ready-made set looks better on stage. See [play money vs prop money](/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/).

## Common mistakes with printed play money

- Printing a realistic note design for a party. Notes that go home in pockets cause trouble. Use clearly pretend designs.

- Not printing enough. Always print a spare set.

- Using thin paper. It rips within one lesson.

- Forgetting the bank. Someone needs a stack of small notes to give change.

## What a ready-made set gives you

A ready-made set from an Australian supplier gives you consistent Australian denominations, heavier paper and a clear play or specimen marking, in a pack that is delivered to your door. The [event and party prop cash pack](/shop/event-and-party-props/event-and-party-prop-cash-pack/) is built for classrooms, parties and games. For larger groups, see the [bulk money stack pack](/shop/money-stacks/bulk-money-stack-pack/). If you are not sure how many you need, read [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) for a counting method that also works for games.

## A realistic cost comparison
Here is a simple way to compare. Suppose you print three sets of notes for a class of 24 shop-game groups. Each set needs about ten sheets of card, so thirty sheets in total, plus colour ink and an hour of cutting. Over a year, with two or three lessons using the notes and some notes torn or lost, you will probably reprint at least once. The effort adds up to several hours. A ready-made set costs more on day one but does not need reprinting, so the total cost often evens out within a term for a busy classroom. For a single party, printing usually wins on price. For repeated use, buying usually wins on time.

## Laminating printed play money
If you choose to print, laminating makes a large difference. A laminated note survives sticky fingers, spills and many rounds of a game. Use a thin pouch so the notes stay flexible, and trim the edges after laminating, leaving a small border so the plastic stays sealed. Laminating does take time and money for pouches, so factor it into the cost. For a class set, many teachers laminate the sheets first and cut afterwards, which is faster than laminating individual notes.

## Choosing a printable design
Look for designs that are clearly cartoon or game-themed. Good play money printouts have large numbers, bright colours and the words play money or similar printed on each note. Avoid templates that reproduce the look of real banknotes closely, because those are the ones that raise legal questions. If a template looks like a photograph of a real note, skip it. Children do not need realistic detail to learn about money, and a clearly pretend design avoids any confusion.

## Custom play money for classrooms and clubs
One real advantage of printing is customisation. A teacher can print notes with the school name, a class mascot or reward values that suit a behaviour system. A club can print notes for a fundraising game. Custom play money like this is a good use of printouts because no ready-made set matches it. If you want a professionally made custom set for a larger project, see our [custom and branded prop currency](/shop/custom-and-branded-props/custom-and-branded-prop-currency/) and the guide for [agencies](/blog/custom-and-branded-prop-currency-guide-for-agencies/).

## Printing for different paper sizes
Most home printers use A4 paper. A4 holds roughly eight to ten notes per sheet depending on the design. Check the print preview so notes are not cut off, and print a single test page before you print the whole batch. If your printer struggles with heavy card, print on standard paper and glue the sheets to thin card afterwards. Make sure each denomination is on a different colour of paper if you can, because colour helps children sort quickly.

## Saving ink
Colour printing eats ink. To save it, choose designs with light backgrounds, print in draft mode for classroom sets and avoid solid blocks of colour. Some free templates offer a black-and-white version that you can print on coloured paper, which gives colour without the ink. This is a good option for large classes.

## When to give up and buy
If you find yourself reprinting every month, cutting at midnight or fielding complaints about torn notes, it is time to buy a set. The time you save is worth more than the purchase price for most teachers and parents. A set that is delivered to your door and lasts for years removes the whole problem. Our [event and party prop cash pack](/shop/event-and-party-props/event-and-party-prop-cash-pack/) is a ready-made option, and larger groups can look at the [bulk money stack pack](/shop/money-stacks/bulk-money-stack-pack/).

### Monopoly Money vs Australian Play Money: What to Use for Games and Parties
- URL: https://aupropmoney.com/blog/monopoly-money-vs-australian-play-money-what-to-use-for-board-games-and-parties/
- Published: 2026-11-28

Monopoly money is the most famous play money in the world. Pastel notes with simple numbers, passed around a board and slowly collected by whoever owns the hotels. Because it is so well known, people search for monopoly money whenever they need pretend cash, even when they are not playing Monopoly. This guide explains what Monopoly money actually is, where it works, where it falls short and when Australian play money is the better choice for a classroom, a party or a game of your own. Monopoly is a registered trademark of its owner, and PROPPS is not connected with the game; we simply sell Australian play and prop money.

## The short answer

Use the money in the box for Monopoly. For everything else, such as a shop game, a classroom, a casino night or a party, use a dedicated play money set with Australian denominations, which is usually larger, clearer and sturdier. Our [Australian play money range](/shop/event-and-party-props/) is built for exactly that.

## What is Monopoly money?

Monopoly money is the paper currency that comes with the board game: coloured notes in a range of denominations, handled by a banker and traded between players. It is designed to be cheap, easy to read and obviously not real. It is the model most people picture when they say play money. The amounts and designs differ between editions and countries, so check the rules in your own box.

## Why people search for monopoly money

The search usually has one of four purposes.

1. Replacing lost notes. A set is missing a few $50s.

2. Looking for a printable. Someone wants to print a spare set.

3. Finding pretend money for another game. A kids' shop, a role play or a party.

4. Learning the rules. How much each player starts with. See our guide on [how much money you start with in Monopoly](/blog/how-much-money-do-you-start-with-in-the-monopoly-game-and-how-to-play-with-more/).

Each need has a different best answer, which is what the rest of this guide covers.

## Monopoly money vs Australian play money

| Question | Monopoly money | Australian play money set |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | One board game | Games, lessons, parties, role play |
| Currency | Game denominations | Familiar Australian denominations |
| Quantity | Whatever is in the box | Chosen by you |
| Durability | Light paper, wears out | Heavier stock, built for handling |
| Look | Pastel, game-themed | Australian-style notes with play marking |
| Replace | Hard to buy separately | Order more any time |

## When Monopoly money is enough

If you are playing Monopoly, use Monopoly money. The notes are matched to the rules, the bank and the pace of the game. There is no reason to swap them unless you have lost many of them.

## When to switch to Australian play money

A classroom shop or maths lesson. Children practise with the notes they will meet in real life. Our guide to [classroom play money](/blog/fake-money-for-classroom-play-money-lessons-by-year-level/) shows how.

A casino or game night. Guests need a float and a way to cash out. See [fake money for parties](/blog/fake-money-for-parties-casino-nights-birthdays-weddings/).

A kids' pretend shop. A set of notes with clear denominations works better than a handful of game bills.

A house rule version of Monopoly. If you want a longer game with more money in circulation, add a set of play money to the bank.

## How many notes does a game need?

For a family board game, the box is designed to fit. For anything else, count the players and decide the float. A table of six playing a shop game needs a float for each player plus a bank for change. A casino night with twenty guests needs twenty floats and a bigger bank. Buy slightly more than the headcount suggests, because a shortage stops the game.

## Keep play money clearly play money

Play money should never be something that could be mistaken for real currency. The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) covers counterfeit currency, and the [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions. Monopoly money passes this test easily because it is obviously a game. Australian play money from a supplier should carry a clear play or specimen marking. PROPPS notes do. Our [compliance page](/compliance/) explains how we build to the standard.

## Replacing lost Monopoly notes

If you have lost a few notes, the cheapest fix is a small play money set in similar denominations. It will not match the colours exactly, but the game works. For a long-lived board game collection, keep a spare set in the box with the rest.

## Monopoly money printable: should you print it?

A printable set can rescue a game night, but it is slow to cut and short-lived. For a one-off game, printing is fine. For regular use, a ready-made set is easier. Our guide to [play money printouts](/blog/play-money-printouts-australia-print-at-home-or-buy-a-ready-made-set/) compares the two.

## Common mistakes

- Using realistic notes for a party game. Guests take notes home. Use play money.

- Running out of small notes. The bank needs plenty of $1 and $5 notes for change.

- Mixing sets without checking denominations. Two sets with different values confuse players.

- Letting children keep notes that look real. Use clearly play notes.

## Where PROPPS fits

We do not sell the board game. We sell Australian play money and prop notes. The [event and party prop cash pack](/shop/event-and-party-props/event-and-party-prop-cash-pack/) is the usual choice for games, classrooms and parties, and the [bulk money stack pack](/shop/money-stacks/bulk-money-stack-pack/) suits larger events. If you need help choosing, [contact the studio](/contact/).

## A short history of play money in games
Play money is as old as board games. Early commercial games used simple paper notes so that players could pass value around the table without confusion. The idea stuck because it works: notes are tactile, easy to count and make a game feel like a real economy. Over time, play money became its own product, sold for classrooms, toy shops, parties and theatre. Monopoly made one style famous, but the category is much wider.

## Why Monopoly money feels the way it does
Monopoly notes are designed to be simple. They use a limited colour scheme, large numbers and little detail. This makes them easy to read across a table and hard to mistake for real currency. The paper is light so the box stays small and cheap. Those design choices suit the game but explain why the notes wear out. When a family plays Monopoly every weekend for years, the notes curl, tear and disappear.

## Ways to extend a long game
Some groups play Monopoly for hours or over several sessions. A longer game needs more money in circulation, and a small play money set helps. A few house rules work well: add a second bank for a variant game, give every player a bonus on a rule-based event, or use the spare notes as a separate pool for a side game. Whatever you choose, agree the rules before you start. Our guide on [how much money you start with](/blog/how-much-money-do-you-start-with-in-the-monopoly-game-and-how-to-play-with-more/) lists common variations.

## Using play money for other board games
Many games use money in some form. Trivia nights can use play money as scoring. Auction games work well with a float for each player. Role-playing games often include a shop where players buy gear. A set of Australian-style notes covers all of these. Keep a spare set in your games cupboard so any group can use it.

## Using play money at school fairs and fundraisers
A fete or fair with play money stalls is a fun way to run a children's area. Each child receives a small amount of play money and can spend it at games and stalls, with each stall giving a small prize. Because the money is clearly play money, it avoids the problems of children handling real cash. Collect the notes at the end and reuse them for the next event. See our guide to [fake money for parties](/blog/fake-money-for-parties-casino-nights-birthdays-weddings/) for event ideas.

## Looking after your set
Wherever you play, store notes flat in a box, sort them by denomination and keep them away from damp. Replace torn notes before they cause arguments. If the set is shared between several households or a club, keep a note of how many notes are in the box so missing ones are noticed quickly.

## Teaching with play money
Teachers often start with the idea of a simple economy. Students earn, save and spend play money, and the class discusses what makes a good price. The same approach works in a family: children can earn play money for chores and spend it on small privileges. It is a gentle introduction to budgeting. If you want a ready-made option for a class, see [fake money for classroom lessons](/blog/fake-money-for-classroom-play-money-lessons-by-year-level/).

### How Much Money Do You Start With in the Monopoly Game (and How to Play With More)
- URL: https://aupropmoney.com/blog/how-much-money-do-you-start-with-in-the-monopoly-game-and-how-to-play-with-more/
- Published: 2026-11-28

How much money do you start with in the Monopoly game? It is one of the most searched game questions, usually asked at the start of an evening when somebody cannot find the rules. This guide gives the standard answer, a note-by-note breakdown, the common house rules that change the amount and a practical way to play a longer or bigger game by adding a set of play money. Rules differ between editions and countries, so always check the rulebook in your own box. Monopoly is a registered trademark of its owner, and PROPPS is not connected with the game.

## The short answer

In the standard edition of Monopoly, each player starts with $1,500 in the game's play money. The banker deals it out before the first roll and keeps the rest in the bank. Some editions, such as quick-play or themed versions, use different amounts, so confirm the number printed in your rulebook. If your set is missing notes, a small play money set from our [Australian range](/shop/event-and-party-props/) can stand in.

## The starting note breakdown

The classic starting hand is usually dealt like this in the standard edition:

| Note | How many | Total |
|---|---|---|
| $500 | 2 | $1,000 |
| $100 | 2 | $200 |
| $50 | 2 | $100 |
| $20 | 6 | $120 |
| $10 | 5 | $50 |
| $5 | 5 | $25 |
| $1 | 5 | $5 |
| Total | | $1,500 |

Check your own edition, because some versions use different splits. The principle is the same: a mix of big notes for property and small notes for rent and change.

## What the banker does

The banker deals each player's starting money, pays salary, collects taxes and sells properties. Experienced players often make the most generous person the banker and let them also play, keeping their own money separate. A tidy bank means the game runs smoothly: sort the notes by value and keep the small ones close at hand.

## Why the amount matters

The starting amount shapes the first half of the game. With $1,500 you can buy two or three properties early and still pay rent. Players who spend everything on the first lap are in trouble when they hit an opponent's hotel. Many family arguments begin with a miscounted bank or a forgotten salary.

## House rules that change the starting money

Families and clubs adjust the game to suit their group.

- A bigger start. Giving every player $2,000 or $3,000 shortens the buying phase and gets people into the trading stage faster.

- A smaller start. A starting amount under $1,500 makes the game tighter and more competitive.

- Free Parking jackpot. Fines and taxes go to the middle of the board and the lucky player gets the pot. This increases money in circulation.

- No auction rule changes. Some groups skip auctions to keep the game quick.

These are house rules, not official rules, so agree them before you start.

## How to run out of money less often

The bank can run out of small notes in a long game. If that happens, you can write IOUs on paper, but it is easier to have spare notes. A set of play money in $1, $5, $10 and $20 notes keeps the game moving. Buy a set in Australian-style denominations and add it to the bank. Our [event and party prop cash pack](/shop/event-and-party-props/event-and-party-prop-cash-pack/) works for this, and the guide to [Monopoly money vs Australian play money](/blog/monopoly-money-vs-australian-play-money-what-to-use-for-board-games-and-parties/) explains the differences.

## Adding play money for a larger game

If you are playing with six or eight people, or running a tournament at a club, the box money may not stretch. Add a play money set and agree on a conversion: for example, treat the extra notes as the same value as the box notes. Mark the added notes by sorting them into their own tray so they do not mix up with the original set.

## Teaching money with Monopoly

Monopoly is also a classroom tool. It teaches counting, change and basic budgeting. A teacher can use the starting money for a lesson: how much is left after buying a property, how much rent is due, how many $50 notes make $500. Our guide to [fake money for classroom lessons](/blog/fake-money-for-classroom-play-money-lessons-by-year-level/) has activities by year level.

## Keep play money clearly play money

Whatever set you use, play money should be obviously play. The [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions, and the [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) covers counterfeit currency. PROPPS notes carry a clear non-legal-tender marking, and our [compliance page](/compliance/) explains the standard.

## Common mistakes in the first five minutes

- Dealing the wrong notes. Check the breakdown against your edition.

- Forgetting the banker keeps their own money separate. It prevents accidental cheating.

- Letting the bank run out of small notes. Keep a spare set.

- Not agreeing house rules. Decide before rolling.

## Setting up the bank before you play
A good game starts with a tidy bank. Before the first roll, sort the notes by denomination in a tray or the box lid. Give each player their starting hand and put the remaining notes in the bank. Place the title deeds, houses and hotels near the banker. A well-organised bank takes two minutes to set up and prevents arguments later.

## How the starting amount changes strategy
The starting amount sets the pace. With the standard $1,500, most players buy the first few properties they land on and aim for a colour set. A smaller start makes players cautious and slows the game down. A larger start encourages early buying and quick development, which can make the game shorter and more aggressive. If your group likes long games, try the standard amount. If you want a faster game, add money.

## Starting hands for different group sizes
With two or three players, the standard amount works well because there is more money in the bank for each person. With six to eight players the bank can get tight, so many groups add a spare set of notes. A small play money set in $1, $5 and $10 notes is ideal because it fills the denominations that run out first. A casual tip: keep the $500 notes for later in the game, when players are building hotels.

## Tracking money during the game
Experienced players keep a mental total. If you lose track, ask the banker for a quick count. For long games, write the starting amount on a sheet of paper and update it after big purchases. Some people use a simple score sheet. Keeping a record also helps settle disputes at the end of the night.

## Variants that use more or less money
Some groups play a speed version where the game ends after a set time and the richest player wins. Others run a tournament where every player starts with the same hand and the lowest-ranked player is eliminated each round. Adding extra notes for a tournament helps because there are more transactions. A larger bank also makes it easier to support a game of eight or ten players.

## What to do if someone runs out of money
Rules for bankruptcy are in the rulebook. In practice, many families allow players to mortgage properties and trade before they are out. If a player runs out of notes because the bank has none left in a denomination, the banker can make change from other notes or use IOUs. Having a spare set avoids that issue.

## Replacing lost starting money
If your starting hand is incomplete, buy a play money set and match the denominations. You do not need to match the colours exactly, but you do want the same values. Keep the replacement notes in a separate bag so you know which are which. Our guide to [Monopoly money amounts](/blog/monopoly-money-amounts-every-denomination-and-how-many-notes-are-in-the-bank/) lists the usual denominations.

## Quick answers before you roll
Most first-time questions come down to a handful of points. Every player starts with the same hand. The banker keeps the bank separate from their own money. Salary is paid each time a player passes Go. Taxes and fines go to the bank unless you use the Free Parking house rule. If a player cannot pay, they sell or mortgage before declaring they are out. Agreeing these points in a minute at the table removes most disputes, and it is worth writing the house rules on a card kept inside the box lid so next game night starts quickly.

## Teaching children the starting hand
Children enjoy dealing the starting money. Ask them to count out the hand into piles by value, then check the total together. It turns the setup into a short counting game. Younger players can use a smaller hand with only $1, $5 and $10 notes, which keeps the numbers friendly. Older children can handle the full range, including large notes. A child who learns to count a $1,500 hand without help has practised addition, grouping and checking, all before the first dice roll.

### Buy Movie Props in Australia: Prop Money, Movie Props for Sale and Where to Look
- URL: https://aupropmoney.com/blog/buy-movie-props-in-australia-prop-money-and-where-to-find-it/
- Published: 2026-11-28

If you need to buy movie props in Australia, the right answer depends on the prop. Furniture, costumes and vehicles are hired from specialist houses. Consumables, set dressing and anything that is used up or damaged on camera are bought. Prop money sits firmly in the second group: it is cheap per note, easy to ship and usually needed in large numbers. This guide explains where Australian productions find movie props for sale, how to decide between buying and hiring, and how to buy prop money for a shoot quickly and legally. It is general information, not legal advice.

## The short answer

For prop money, buy it from a supplier that sells non-legal-tender notes with specimen markings, in the denominations and quantities your scene needs. Browse the [film and TV prop currency](/shop/film-and-tv-props/) and place your order early so delivery does not hold up the shoot.

## Buying vs hiring movie props

Not every prop should be bought. A useful rule: if you will return it, hire it; if you will use it up, mark it or lose it, buy it.

- Hire: vehicles, large furniture, costumes, specialist equipment, high-value antiques.

- Buy: consumables, weathered or damaged items, branded items, lots of small props and prop money.

Prop money is a classic buy. Notes get handled, stacked, thrown, burnt in a story and sometimes lost. A film production would rather buy a stack than chase returns.

## Where Australian productions find movie props for sale

- Prop houses. Specialist hire houses in Melbourne and Sydney have large stock, with some items for sale.

- Specialist suppliers. Companies that make or source one category, such as prop currency, firearms replicas or signage.

- Online marketplaces. Useful for small items, but check seller details and returns.

- Production offcuts and sales. Occasional sales when a show wraps.

- Local makers. Props built to order for a particular script.

For prop currency, a specialist supplier is the best choice because the marking, the legal checks and the quantity pricing are built in. Our guide to [buying film props in Australia: a checklist for art departments](/blog/buying-film-props-in-australia-a-checklist-for-art-departments/) covers the wider process.

## Prop money: what to order

Think about the scene, not the shop. Decide the denominations, the quantity, the look and the camera distance.

1. Denominations. Choose notes that suit the story: $50 and $100 for a payoff, $20 for everyday cash. Our guide to the [best Australian banknote denominations for film and TV scenes](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) helps.

2. Quantity. A hand-held bundle is not the same as a briefcase. See [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/).

3. Condition. Crisp notes for a bank scene, aged notes for a street deal. Read the [art department guide to weathering prop cash](/blog/art-department-guide-weathering-prop-cash/).

4. Camera distance. Close-ups need the most realistic notes; wide shots forgive more.

5. Spares. Order 10 to 20 percent more to cover damage and reshoots.

## The legal side of movie prop money

Realistic prop money is legal to buy and use on a production when it is a clearly marked reproduction made for that purpose. The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) targets counterfeit currency, and the [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions. Productions should keep notes on set, count them in and out, and never let them leave the production. Our [compliance page](/compliance/) and the guide to [Section 22 and the RBA prop money guidelines](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) explain how PROPPS builds to the standard.

## How to brief a prop money supplier

A good brief saves days. Include:

1. The production name and the dates on set.

2. The scenes that use cash and what happens to it.

3. The denominations and rough quantities.

4. The delivery address and when you need it.

5. Whether you need an invoice for the art department or the production company.

If you are unsure about quantities, [contact the studio](/contact/) and we will help you size the order.

## Budgeting for prop money

Prop money is a small line in a production budget, but it is easy to under-order. Count the number of scenes, the number of takes and the places where notes can be damaged. Order enough to reset between takes. For larger shows, the [bulk money stack pack](/shop/money-stacks/bulk-money-stack-pack/) and our [wholesale options](/wholesale/) reduce the cost per note. The guide to [wholesale prop money for production companies](/blog/wholesale-prop-money-for-production-companies-bulk-pricing-explained/) explains pricing.

## Delivery timing

Productions often need props quickly. PROPPS ships from Eltham, Melbourne by Australia Post Express with a signature on delivery. Order early in the week of prep, not the day before the shoot. See the [shipping policy](/shipping-policy/) for times and our guide on [how fast you can get prop money in Australia](/blog/shipping-and-dispatch-how-fast-can-you-get-prop-money-in-australia/).

## Common mistakes when buying movie props

- Ordering the day before. Allow delivery time.

- Buying too few notes. Resets use more than you expect.

- Buying only for the hero shot. Background cash needs notes too.

- Ignoring paperwork. Keep the invoice with the production file.

- Letting notes leave the set. Count them back in every day.

## Planning your prop purchases
Good prop buying starts with the script. Read each scene and list every item that will be handled, thrown, damaged or consumed. For each item, decide whether you will hire it, buy it or make it. Prop money almost always lands in the buy category. Put a quantity next to each item, add a buffer and set a delivery date a week before shooting. A short list, shared with the production manager, avoids last-minute panic.

## Working with a supplier
Treat your supplier as part of the art department. Send a clear brief, ask about lead times and agree how orders will be invoiced. A supplier who understands film can answer questions about markings, quantities and legal compliance without delay. Ask whether they offer volume pricing, because that matters on larger productions. Keep their contact details on the call sheet so any last-minute changes can be handled quickly.

## Short films, music videos and student productions
Not every project has a big budget. For a short film or student production, the prop list is small and the budget tight. In these cases a single stack of notes is often enough. Plan the scenes so you can reuse the same notes in different set-ups. For music videos, notes are often thrown in the air or fanned out, so bring a spare stack. See [prop money for music videos in Australia](/blog/prop-money-for-music-videos-in-australia/) for tips on handling notes in motion.

## Theatre and live performance
Theatre productions also need prop money. The notes are seen from a distance, but they are handled repeatedly and must survive a whole season. Choose heavier notes and plan to replace a few each week. For community theatre, a small set is often enough. For larger productions, order extras for understudies and rehearsals.

## Photography and advertising shoots
Photographers and advertising agencies often need prop money for a single day. Close-up shots need the most realistic notes, but the marking must remain visible so the image can be presented honestly. Our guide to [prop money for photography](/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/) covers lighting and presentation, and [custom and branded prop currency](/shop/custom-and-branded-props/custom-and-branded-prop-currency/) is available for campaigns that need a specific look.

## Storing and returning props
After the shoot, count the notes and store them flat in a labelled box. Keep a record of what was used. Props that were not damaged can be kept for the next job. Damaged notes can be discarded. If your production uses a standard prop store, label the money box with the production name and date. A good record helps if the same props are needed for reshoots.

## Why buy from a local supplier
A local supplier cuts delivery times and makes returns and queries simple. You can phone or email someone who understands Australian productions, and invoices are in Australian dollars. Overseas suppliers may be cheaper per note but add shipping delays and customs risk. Our article on [local vs overseas prop money suppliers](/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/) explains the trade-offs.

## A simple order timeline
Work backwards from the first shooting day. Four weeks out, finalise the list of props and quantities. Three weeks out, send briefs to suppliers and confirm prices. Two weeks out, place the order and arrange delivery to the art department, not to a private address. One week out, check the delivery and test the notes under the lights. Shooting day, count the notes out to the set and back in at wrap. This rhythm suits features, short films and commercials, and it leaves a week to fix anything that arrives wrong.

## Questions art departments ask first
Productions usually ask three things: can the notes be aged, can they be matched later, and can we get an invoice in the production company name. The answers are yes for a good supplier. Ask early, because custom aging or branded notes take longer than stock items. If you need a particular look, send a reference image and the camera distance so the supplier can recommend the right product.
