### Toy Shop Money Games: Play Money for Pretend Shops and Kids Learning
- URL: https://aupropmoney.com/blog/toy-shop-money-games-play-money-for-pretend-shops-and-kids-learning/
- Published: 2026-11-28

A toy shop money game is one of the oldest and best ways to teach children about money: a table, a few toys with price tags, a till and a pile of notes. Children play shopkeeper and customer, count out payments and work out change without realising they are doing maths. This guide shows how to set up a toy shop money game at home or in a classroom, how much play money you need, how to run the game for different ages and what to look for when you buy a set. It is general information, and every note we mention is clearly play money.

## The short answer

For a shop game you need three things: items with simple prices, a shopkeeper's till with change, and a set of play money for the customers. A mixed set of Australian-style notes in $5, $10, $20, $50 and $100 is enough for most games. The [event and party prop cash pack](/shop/event-and-party-props/event-and-party-prop-cash-pack/) is the set we recommend for pretend shops. Keep the notes in a box, count them back in at the end and replace torn ones.

## What you need for a toy shop money game

1. Items to sell. Toys, books, cups, anything small. Keep it to ten or fewer.

2. Price tags. Use sticky labels with simple numbers such as $2, $5 and $10.

3. A till or tray. A shoebox with sections for each denomination works.

4. Play money. Notes for the customers and a bank for the shopkeeper.

5. A bag or basket. For the shopping.

6. A small notebook. For the shopkeeper to record sales if the children are older.

## How much play money do you need?

Plan by players and by price range.

| Players | Price range | Suggested play money |
|---|---|---|
| 2 children | Up to $10 | One mixed set |
| 4 children | Up to $20 | One mixed set per pair, plus a till bank |
| Class of 24 | Up to $50 | Six or more sets plus a teacher's bank |
| Party of 10 | Up to $20 | Float per child plus a till |

The most common mistake is not having enough small notes. The shopkeeper needs plenty of $5 and $10 notes for change. If you run out of small notes, the game stops while someone tries to break a $50.

## How to run the game by age

Ages 3 to 4. Do not worry about exact amounts. Let them hand over one note for one toy and practise saying thank you. The goal is the idea of exchange.

Ages 5 to 6. Use prices up to $10 and let children count notes. Prices of $1, $2 and $5 work well. Introduce the idea of change by letting the shopkeeper give back a note.

Ages 7 to 8. Prices up to $50. Customers choose several items and add them up. The shopkeeper checks the total and the change.

Ages 9 and over. Add discounts, a sale sign, a budget and a loyalty card. Students can record sales and calculate profit. See our guide to [fake money for classroom lessons by year level](/blog/fake-money-for-classroom-play-money-lessons-by-year-level/).

## Rules that keep the game fun

- Swap roles. Every child takes a turn as shopkeeper.

- Count aloud. It builds number sense and catches mistakes.

- Check change together. The shopkeeper counts back from the price to the note handed over.

- Tidy up as a team. Sort notes by value and count them back in.

- Play money stays in the game. It is never used to pay for anything real.

## Turning the game into learning

A shop game becomes a maths lesson with small changes.

1. Price puzzles. Give each child $20 and ask what they could buy.

2. Two-step problems. Buy two items and work out the change.

3. Budget challenges. Spend as close to $50 as you can without going over.

4. Sale days. Half price on Friday. Children recalculate prices.

5. Profit. The shopkeeper buys stock at one price and sells at another.

Our guide to [toy money and play money for kids' games and learning](/blog/toy-money-and-play-money-for-kids-games-and-learning/) has more ideas, and the article on [monetary toys and play money sets](/blog/monetary-toys-and-play-money-sets-for-kids/) explains which types suit which ages.

## Choosing play money for a shop game

Look for a few key things.

1. Australian denominations. Children learn the values they will see in real life.

2. Clear play marking. The notes should be obviously not real currency. PROPPS notes carry a specimen marking.

3. Sturdy paper. Children handle notes a lot.

4. Enough small notes. For change.

5. A supplier that ships in Australia. With an invoice and tracking.

Compare options in our guides to [Kmart play money vs a prop supplier](/blog/play-money-kmart-vs-a-prop-money-supplier-what-to-buy-in-australia/) and [play money printouts](/blog/play-money-printouts-australia-print-at-home-or-buy-a-ready-made-set/).

## Safety and the law

Play money should be clearly play. The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) covers counterfeit currency, and the [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions. A children's set with a play marking and a design that is not a copy of a real note is the safe choice. Our [compliance page](/compliance/) explains how PROPPS builds to the standard.

## Setting up a classroom or party toy shop

For a class, set up three or four stations, each with its own shopkeeper and till. Rotate children every ten minutes. For a party, run the shop as an activity: each child gets a float and a bag, and they shop for small prizes. At the end, count the notes back in, and everyone takes home a prize. A shop game also works for fundraisers and school fetes, when children play the shopkeepers.

## Common mistakes

- Too many items. Ten is plenty.

- Prices that are too hard. Match prices to age.

- No change in the till. Give the shopkeeper small notes.

- Letting the game drag on. Fifteen to twenty minutes is enough for young children.

- Forgetting to count back. Missing notes are the most common complaint.

## Shop themes that kids love
A toy shop money game works with almost any theme. A grocery store with plastic food, a cafe with a menu, a bakery with cardboard cakes, a pet shop with soft toys and a bookshop all work well. Let the children choose the theme and make the signs. A cafe lets you add a menu with prices, which is great practice for reading numbers. A bank theme adds another level because one child can act as the teller and change notes into smaller ones.

## Making price tags and signs
Children enjoy making price tags. Use sticky labels or cards, and write prices in large numbers. For younger children, keep prices as whole dollars. For older children, include cents so they practise decimals. A sale sign with a percentage is a fun challenge for students who are learning fractions. Display a price list near the till so the shopkeeper can check totals quickly.

## Giving change step by step
Giving change is the heart of a shop game, and it is a skill many adults still find tricky. Teach the counting-up method: start at the price and count up to the amount handed over. If an item costs $7 and the customer gives a $10 note, the shopkeeper says seven, then adds $1 notes or a $2 coin: eight, nine, ten. This method works with any amount and builds mental maths. Practise it with low prices first.

## Playing with siblings of different ages
When children of different ages play together, give the older child the role of banker or manager and let the younger child be the customer. The older child can check totals and help with change. Alternatively, give younger children simple prices and older children harder ones. Everyone gets a turn at both roles. Keep sessions short so the youngest does not lose interest.

## Extending the game with a bank
Adding a bank makes the game richer. Children can deposit notes, withdraw cash and earn pretend interest. The bank teller keeps a ledger, which brings in reading and writing. A bank needs a set of small notes for change, so a larger set is useful. See the [bulk money stack pack](/shop/money-stacks/bulk-money-stack-pack/) for classroom-sized quantities.

## Tidying and counting back
Make cleaning up part of the game. At the end, the shopkeeper counts the takings and the customers count what is left. Compare totals: the money in the till plus the money in customers' hands should equal the starting amount. If it does not, children enjoy detective work to find the missing notes. This turns tidy-up into a counting exercise and teaches that money does not disappear.

## Beyond the shop
Once children are comfortable, move on to other money games. Run a class market where children make crafts and sell them. Set up a restaurant with orders and bills. Run a travel agency with ticket prices. Each theme uses the same skills in a new setting. A good set of play money supports them all, and the guide to [toy money and play money for kids](/blog/toy-money-and-play-money-for-kids-games-and-learning/) has more ideas.

## Where to go next

Browse the [Australian play money range](/shop/event-and-party-props/), see the [event and party prop cash pack](/shop/event-and-party-props/event-and-party-prop-cash-pack/) or [contact the studio](/contact/) for classroom quantities. PROPPS orders start at the $150 AUD minimum, delivery is free from $500 AUD and cryptocurrency payments receive a 10% discount. We invoice and ship from Eltham, Melbourne by [Australia Post Express](https://auspost.com.au/) with a signature on delivery. See the [shipping policy](/shipping-policy/) for times and the [refund policy](/refund-policy/) for the 3 to 8 business day refund window.

### Bundle of Money Props: How Prop Cash Bundles and Stacks Are Made and Used
- URL: https://aupropmoney.com/blog/bundle-of-money-prop-cash-bundles-and-stacks-for-film-photos-and-events/
- Published: 2026-11-28

A bundle of money is one of the strongest images in film and photography: a neat block of notes held together with a paper strap, ready to be handed across a table or dropped on a desk. Searches for a bundle of money are usually about one of two things, a film or photo prop, or how a real cash bundle is described in a story or game. This guide covers the prop side: how prop cash bundles are built, how many notes to include, which denominations look best on camera and where to buy them in Australia. Every product described is a non-legal-tender prop with specimen markings.

## The short answer

A prop bundle is a stack of prop notes held with a band or strap so it holds its shape. For film and photography, buy ready-made bundles rather than making them, so every one looks the same and the notes are marked. The [bulk money stack pack](/shop/money-stacks/bulk-money-stack-pack/) is our stack product for productions and shoots, and the [film and TV prop currency pack](/shop/film-and-tv-props/) suits scenes with fewer notes.

## What is a bundle of money?

In everyday language a bundle of money is a bunch of notes tied together. In film, a bundle is built to read at a glance: stack height, a strap around the middle and often a top note that shows the denomination. The look suggests a specific amount, so it needs to be consistent with the story. A bundle in a bank scene looks different from a handful of crumpled notes in a street deal.

## How prop bundles are built

Prop bundles are usually built from three parts.

1. The notes. Marked prop notes in the right denomination.

2. The strap. A paper band around the middle to hold the stack. Bands are often colour-coded by value in a bank setting.

3. The top note. Real prop notes on the top and bottom, with plain paper or cheaper notes in the middle for weight and to reduce cost in some productions.

Ready-made bundles from a supplier save time and give you a consistent look across scenes. If you build your own, keep the marked notes visible and never let unmarked paper imitate real currency.

## How many notes in a bundle?

A common bank-style bundle holds 100 notes. A smaller prop bundle may hold 25, 50 or more depending on the story and the camera. The number of notes on screen determines the sense of the value: a bundle of 100 $50 notes reads as $5,000. For heist and bank scenes, count the notes you can see and match them to the script. Our guide to [prop cash for heist and bank scenes](/blog/prop-cash-for-heist-and-bank-scenes-getting-the-volume-right/) explains the maths, and [how much is a million dollars in prop money](/blog/how-much-is-a-million-dollars-in-prop-money/) shows how fast the numbers grow.

## Which denominations look best?

| Denomination | Best for |
|---|---|
| $100 | Big payoffs, close-ups, heist cash |
| $50 | Everyday criminal cash, office payoffs |
| $20 | Street deals, tips, bar scenes |
| $10 and $5 | Background cash, shop tills |

For wide shots, any denomination reads as cash. For close-ups, choose the denomination that matches the scene. See the [best Australian banknote denominations for film and TV scenes](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/).

## Bundle of money for photography and content

A single bundle is a strong photo prop. Place it on a clean surface, light it from the side to avoid glare and add a caption that makes clear the money is a prop. Our guide to [prop money for photography](/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/) explains the set-up, and the [lighting guide](/blog/lighting-prop-money-for-camera-avoiding-glare/) helps with reflections. Content creators should read the [guidelines for social media and photoshoots](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/).

## Bundle of money for events and parties

At parties, bundles are used in photo booths, as table decorations and as prizes. For an event, use clearly play notes, not realistic ones. Bundles of realistic notes can leave the venue in a guest's bag. See [fake money for parties](/blog/fake-money-for-parties-casino-nights-birthdays-weddings/) for safe set-ups.

## Keep every bundle clearly a prop

Whatever the use, prop bundles must be clearly props. The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) covers counterfeit currency, and the [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions. PROPPS notes carry specimen markings, and our [compliance page](/compliance/) explains the standard. Never use a prop bundle as payment, never post it with a caption suggesting real cash and keep bundles on set or in storage.

## Storing and handling bundles

Store bundles flat in a dry box. Remove bands before long storage to avoid permanent creases. Keep a count of bundles in and out on a production. If a bundle is damaged, replace it rather than repairing it, because a patched note looks wrong on camera.

## Buying a bundle of money in Australia

Order from an Australian prop supplier that issues an invoice and ships with tracking. PROPPS ships from Eltham, Melbourne by Express Post with a signature on delivery. For many bundles, check the [bulk pack](/shop/money-stacks/bulk-money-stack-pack/) and our [wholesale options](/wholesale/). The guide to [ready prop money stacks for fast turnaround](/blog/ready-prop-money-stacks-for-fast-turnaround/) shows how quickly an order can be arranged.

## Common mistakes with prop bundles

- Using too few notes. A thin stack looks cheap.

- Mismatching the denomination and the story. A suitcase of $5 notes is not a ransom.

- Forgetting spares. Bundles get damaged on set.

- Letting bundles leave the set. Count them back in.

## Bank straps and what the colours mean
Real bank bundles use paper straps, and some banks colour-code the straps by denomination. In a film, you do not need to match any specific bank's system, but a consistent colour for each denomination helps the audience read the scene. Choose a strap that is a plain, neutral colour unless the story needs a specific look. Avoid straps that carry the logo of a real bank without permission. A plain strap with a printed value is safe and looks professional.

## Building a bundle that reads on camera
The camera sees the edge of the stack more than the top. A bundle with clean, aligned edges looks like new money. A bundle with ragged edges looks used. Decide which look you want. For a close-up, make sure the strap sits straight and the top note faces the camera. For a pile of bundles, stack them in a neat pattern, because messy piles look like a prop department did them in a hurry. Use a ruler or a small jig to keep edges straight.

## Weight and handling
A real bundle of 100 notes has weight. An actor who handles a light stack may move it too easily and break the illusion. Ask the performer to handle the stack as if it were heavy, and choose a stack that is dense enough to feel real. A briefcase of bundles is heavy too, so test it before the scene. If the briefcase is going to be thrown or dropped, make sure the bundles are secure.

## Aged and weathered bundles
For gritty scenes, use bundles with some wear. Weathered notes look more realistic in a crime story. See the [art department guide to weathering prop cash](/blog/art-department-guide-weathering-prop-cash/) for techniques, and test a sample bundle under the lights before committing. The risk is over-ageing, so work in small steps.

## Photographing bundles
Photographers should shoot at an angle so the strap and the edges are visible. Use soft lighting from the side to reduce glare on the paper. Place the bundle on a neutral surface, and leave space around it for text if the image will be used in design. The marking on the note should remain readable, which keeps the image honest. See [lighting prop money for camera](/blog/lighting-prop-money-for-camera-avoiding-glare/).

## Counting bundles on set
On a production, bundles are easy to lose. Number each bundle on its strap with a small mark that does not show on camera, keep a sheet listing the numbers and check them in and out at the start and end of each day. If a bundle goes missing, you will know which one and when. This habit takes seconds and saves worry.

## Budgeting for many bundles
Bundles add up quickly. A set with fifty bundles of 100 notes needs 5,000 notes, so the supplier's volume pricing matters. Our [wholesale page](/wholesale/) and the [bulk money stack pack](/shop/money-stacks/bulk-money-stack-pack/) are built for that scale. If you are unsure, send the supplier your scene list, and they can estimate the stack count.

## Quick checklist before you buy bundles
Decide the denomination, the number of bundles, the strap style, the camera distance and the delivery date. Check that every note carries the specimen marking. Ask for an invoice. Order a few extra bundles for spares. Plan where the bundles will be stored on set and who is responsible for counting them. A short checklist like this takes five minutes and prevents the usual surprises on the shooting day.

## Where to go next

See the [bulk money stack pack](/shop/money-stacks/bulk-money-stack-pack/), the [film and TV prop currency pack](/shop/film-and-tv-props/) or [contact the studio](/contact/) with your quantities. PROPPS orders start at the $150 AUD minimum, delivery is free from $500 AUD and cryptocurrency payments receive a 10% discount. We invoice and ship from Eltham, Melbourne by [Australia Post Express](https://auspost.com.au/) with a signature on delivery. See the [shipping policy](/shipping-policy/) for times and the [refund policy](/refund-policy/) for the 3 to 8 business day refund window.

### Fake Money for Film: What Productions Should Use and How to Buy It Legally in Australia
- URL: https://aupropmoney.com/blog/fake-money-for-film-what-productions-should-use-and-how-to-buy-it-legally/
- Published: 2026-11-28

When filmmakers search for fake money for film, they usually mean prop money: notes that look right on camera but are not real currency. The wording matters, because fake money can also mean counterfeit notes, which are a crime to make or use. This guide explains the difference in plain language, what Australian productions actually use on set, how to buy it legally and how to handle it so it never causes problems. It is general information, not legal advice. Every product we sell is a non-legal-tender prop carrying specimen markings.

## The short answer

For a film, buy prop money: marked, non-legal-tender notes made as props. Do not buy anything sold as counterfeit or designed to pass as real. Order from an Australian supplier that issues an invoice, and keep the notes on set. Browse our [film and TV prop currency](/shop/film-and-tv-props/) or read the guide to [fake money vs prop money in Australia](/blog/fake-money-vs-prop-money-the-legal-difference-in-australia/).

## Fake money vs prop money: the difference that matters

People use fake money loosely. In a legal and professional sense there are two very different things.

- Counterfeit money. Notes made to be passed as real. Making, possessing or using them is a serious offence under the Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/). No production should touch them.

- Prop money. Reproductions made for motion pictures, television, theatre and similar uses, clearly marked as props and not intended to deceive. The [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions.

Our products are prop money. They carry specimen markings, and we never market them as spendable. Read the [compliance page](/compliance/) for how we build to the standard.

## What Australian productions use on set

Most productions use a mix.

1. Hero notes. The most realistic notes for close-ups, handled by actors.

2. Stacks and bundles. For tables, bags and briefcases. See [bundle of money props](/blog/bundle-of-money-prop-cash-bundles-and-stacks-for-film-photos-and-events/).

3. Aged notes. Weathered for street scenes. See the [art department guide to weathering prop cash](/blog/art-department-guide-weathering-prop-cash/).

4. Background cash. Lower-detail notes for wide shots and extras.

5. Play-style notes. For scenes where clearly pretend money is fine, such as kids' productions.

## How to buy fake money for film legally

Follow a simple process.

1. Pick a reputable Australian supplier. Look for an invoice, tracking and clear compliance information.

2. Check the markings. Notes should carry a visible non-legal-tender marking.

3. Choose denominations for the story. See the [best banknote denominations for film and TV](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/).

4. Order enough, plus spares. See [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/).

5. Keep the paperwork. File the invoice with the production's records.

## On-set rules for prop money

- Count notes in and out every day. A missing bundle is a problem.

- Keep notes on set or in the art department. Never leave them in a car or at a cafe.

- Brief the cast and crew. Everyone should know the cash is a prop.

- Tell location owners. If you are filming in a bank, shop or street, tell the owner and local police if needed.

- Never use prop money as payment. Not even as a joke.

## Filming in public with prop money

Shooting on location with realistic cash can attract attention. Have the production notice ready, inform venue staff and keep a copy of the invoice with the production file. Our guide to [Section 22 and the RBA prop money guidelines](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) explains how to present prop money honestly.

## Budget and quantities

Prop money is a small line in a budget but easy to under-order. Count the scenes, the takes and the places where notes get damaged. Larger productions use the [bulk money stack pack](/shop/money-stacks/bulk-money-stack-pack/) and the [wholesale options](/wholesale/). The article on [wholesale prop money for production companies](/blog/wholesale-prop-money-for-production-companies-bulk-pricing-explained/) explains pricing.

## Independent filmmakers and students

A student film or music video needs the same careful approach on a smaller scale. A single stack is often enough. See [prop money for music videos in Australia](/blog/prop-money-for-music-videos-in-australia/) and the [guidelines for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/). The minimum order is $150 AUD, which covers a starter stack plus extras.

## Common mistakes when buying fake money for film

- Buying from an unknown seller. Without an invoice you cannot show it was a prop.

- Choosing counterfeit-style notes. That is the opposite of what a production needs.

- Under-ordering. Resets use more than expected.

- Leaving notes unattended. Count them back in.

## Why wording matters
Search engines and customers use the phrase fake money for film because it is natural language. But professional film people talk about prop money, and the difference is more than a word. Using the correct term shows that you understand the legal position. When you email a supplier, ask for prop money or film prop currency. When you write the production notes, call it prop money. This protects you if anyone asks questions about the notes on set.

## What makes prop money suitable for film
Good film prop money has four qualities. First, the look: it should read as realistic from the camera distance used. Second, the handling: notes should be durable enough for repeated takes. Third, the marking: a visible specimen or non-legal-tender mark keeps the item clearly a prop. Fourth, the supply: you should be able to reorder the same notes if you need more. A supplier that covers all four makes your job easier.

## Talking to your locations department
Locations managers appreciate being told about prop money in advance. If you are shooting in a bank, shop, cafe or street, tell the owner what you will be using. Share a copy of your supplier's compliance page and the invoice. Many venue owners relax when they see the notes are clearly marked props. For public shoots, some productions notify local police as a courtesy.

## Safe handling for cast and crew
Brief everyone who handles the notes. Actors should know the notes are props and must not be taken home. Crew should know not to move notes between locations unless the production manager approves. Keep notes in a locked box when not in use. At wrap, count everything back in. If the count is short, find the missing notes before leaving the location.

## Using prop money on social media
Productions often post behind-the-scenes images. If a post shows prop money, add a caption that makes clear the notes are props. This protects the production from complaints and keeps your brand honest. Our [guidelines for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/) explain how to do it well.

## Low-budget and student films
A student film with a tight budget can still do this properly. Buy one stack in the denominations you need, plan the scenes to reuse the notes and keep careful records. The minimum order is $150 AUD, and we can recommend a quantity if you describe your scenes. [Contact the studio](/contact/) with the script pages that use cash, and we will suggest a sensible size.

## Planning for reshoots
Reshoots are common, and prop money gets damaged. Order a small buffer at the start and keep the notes in good condition. If you need to match notes from the original shoot, keep a sample so you can describe them to the supplier. Reordering the same product from the same supplier is the easiest way to match.

## After the shoot
When the production wraps, store the notes with the other props or return unused stock to the supplier if their policy allows. Check the [refund policy](/refund-policy/) for details. Keep the invoice with the production records so the purchase is documented.

## Frequently confused terms
Several terms get mixed up when people search. Prop money is a marked reproduction made for productions. Play money is a toy or game currency that is clearly not realistic. Novelty money is a joke or gift item. Counterfeit money is made to deceive and is illegal. Movie money is a casual phrase that usually means prop money. Knowing which term you mean helps you choose the right product and explain it to anyone who asks. If you are ever unsure, describe your scene to the supplier and ask them to recommend the correct product.

## What to put in your production paperwork
Keep three documents together: the supplier invoice, a note from the art department listing the quantities and where the notes are used, and the supplier's compliance statement. If a location owner, police officer or insurer asks about the cash on set, you can hand over the paperwork and settle the question in a minute. It is a small habit that shows professionalism, and it protects both the production and the supplier.

### Night at the Casino Party: Play Money, Games and Setup for a Casino Night
- URL: https://aupropmoney.com/blog/night-at-the-casino-party-play-money-games-and-setup-for-a-casino-night/
- Published: 2026-11-28

A night at the casino is one of the easiest themed parties to run: dim lights, a few card tables, a roulette wheel and a pile of play money. Guests dress up, play for pretend stakes and compete for prizes. The play money is the part that makes it feel real without any real gambling. This guide explains how to plan a night at the casino party with play money, how many notes each guest needs, which games work, how to run the bank and how to keep the whole thing safe, legal and fun. It is general information, and every note we mention is clearly play money, never for betting with real value.

## The short answer

Give every guest a starting float of play money, run three or four games and finish with a prize draw where the guest with the most play money wins a prize you supply. Do not allow real money to change hands. A set of Australian play money notes in several denominations covers most parties. The [event and party prop cash pack](/shop/event-and-party-props/event-and-party-prop-cash-pack/) is built for this, and the [bulk money stack pack](/shop/money-stacks/bulk-money-stack-pack/) suits larger groups.

## Keep the night as play only

A casino night is a game, not gambling. Guests should never bet real money, and the play money should have no cash value. If you plan to run raffles or sell tickets for real prizes, check the rules in your state or territory, because fundraising and gaming laws differ. The relevant state regulator can explain what is allowed. For a private party with a prize you supply, a play money game is simply a game.

## How much play money does each guest need?

Plan a float large enough for a few hours of play.

| Guests | Starting float per guest | Notes to buy |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | $1,000 in mixed notes | One set per guest plus a bank |
| 20 | $1,000 in mixed notes | Two bulk packs |
| 40 | $500 in mixed notes | Bulk packs plus the cashier's bank |

Use higher floats for longer parties. The cashier needs a bank of small notes to change big ones. Our guide to [fake money for parties](/blog/fake-money-for-parties-casino-nights-birthdays-weddings/) covers more party types.

## Games to run

1. Blackjack. Easy to learn, needs one dealer per table.

2. Poker. Texas hold'em with fixed blinds is a favourite.

3. Roulette. Needs a wheel and a croupier.

4. Dice games. Easy for guests who do not know cards.

5. Wheel of fortune. A simple prize wheel for the end of the night.

Hire a dealer or ask a friend who knows the games. Put the rules on a card at each table.

## Running the bank

The cashier is the most important role. They give each guest their float at the start, change notes when needed and track the total in the bank. Use a table with a cash box, sorted notes and a simple log. At the end of the night, the cashier counts each guest's play money and announces the winner.

## Prizes

Prizes keep guests competing. Choose prizes that suit your crowd: vouchers, drinks, small gifts or a trophy. A common format is a final leaderboard, with the top three winning prizes and a lucky draw for everyone else. Keep prizes separate from the play money so the money stays purely pretend.

## Dress code and decoration

A casino night is partly about atmosphere. Ask guests to dress formally, dim the lights and use red and black table covers. Stacks of play money on tables add to the look. For photos, see the [photography prop currency set](/shop/photography-props/photography-prop-currency-set/) and the guide on [prop money for photography](/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/).

## Choose clearly pretend notes

For parties, use obviously play notes. Realistic reproductions are fine on a film set but not at a party where notes can end up in pockets and handbags. The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) covers counterfeit currency, and the [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions. PROPPS notes carry a clear non-legal-tender marking. Our [compliance page](/compliance/) explains the standard, and the guide to [novelty money for parties and events](/blog/novelty-money-for-parties-and-events-whats-legal-in-australia/) shows what is safe.

## A simple timeline

1. Doors open (7 pm). Guests collect their float and a drink.

2. Games (7:30 to 10 pm). Rotate between tables.

3. Break (9 pm). Food and photos.

4. Final round (10 pm). Announce the last hour of play.

5. Count and prizes (10:30 pm). Count the notes, announce winners.

6. Collect everything. Gather all play money so none goes home by accident.

## Cleaning up and storing the money

Count all notes back in, bag them by denomination and keep them for your next event. Note any damaged ones and replace them before the next party. A set that is stored flat and dry lasts for many events.

## Casino night for workplaces and fundraisers

Corporate casino nights follow the same format. Give each employee a float, run a few tables and award prizes. For a charity night, check state rules on raffles and fundraising before you sell tickets. A play money game with prizes supplied by sponsors is the simplest route. [Contact the studio](/contact/) if you need larger quantities or branded notes, and see our guide to [custom and branded prop currency](/blog/custom-and-branded-prop-currency-guide-for-agencies/).

## Common mistakes

- Too little money per guest. Guests run out within an hour.

- No small notes in the bank. The cashier cannot change.

- Realistic notes at a loose party. Use clearly play notes.

- Forgetting to count back. Missing notes cause arguments.

- Using real money. Keep it purely pretend.

## Choosing a venue and layout
A casino night works in a living room, a hall, a backyard or a hired space. Set up tables in a loose circle so guests can move between games. Put the cashier near the entrance so guests collect their float on arrival and cash out on the way out. Leave room around each table for spectators. A good layout keeps traffic flowing and stops one table from blocking another.

## Dealers and game masters
Each table needs someone who knows the game. Ask friends who play cards, hire professional dealers or use a short rules card and let guests take turns. Dealers should be briefed on the house rules, including maximum bets and what happens when a guest runs out of play money. A friendly game master who walks around and helps beginners keeps the night fun for everyone.

## House rules that keep the peace
Set simple rules and display them. Examples: each guest receives the same float, play money has no cash value, no real money is used, prizes are supplied by the host, and the cashier's count is final. If a guest runs out of play money, they can either watch, help deal or buy a second float for a small charity donation. Keep the tone light, and make sure everyone understands it is a game.

## Food, drink and responsible hosting
Serve food that is easy to eat with one hand, such as finger food and canapes. If you serve alcohol, follow responsible service rules and make sure guests have a way home. Provide non-alcoholic drinks. A casino night should feel like a stylish party, not a competition to drink. Keep an eye on guests who are getting carried away, even with pretend money.

## Music and atmosphere
Music sets the tone. A playlist of jazz, swing or classic film themes suits the casino mood. Keep the volume low enough for conversation. Add low lighting, table lamps and a few decorations in red, black and gold. A photo corner with a stack of play money and a backdrop gives guests a place to take pictures. Our [photography prop set](/shop/photography-props/photography-prop-currency-set/) is designed for photo props, and the guide to [prop money for photography](/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/) covers set-up.

## Budget and shopping list
A basic casino night needs play money, playing cards, dice, chips if you want them, table covers and prizes. The play money is the main cost. For small groups, one or two sets is enough. For larger groups, order extra so the cashier has a good bank. Our [event and party prop cash pack](/shop/event-and-party-props/event-and-party-prop-cash-pack/) and the [bulk money stack pack](/shop/money-stacks/bulk-money-stack-pack/) cover most needs, and the minimum order is $150 AUD.

## Variations
Try a Great Gatsby theme with 1920s dress, a James Bond evening with martinis and black tie, a Vegas party with neon decorations or a pirate-themed game with treasure. The same play money works for all of them. For children, run a casino-themed fair with prizes and no betting, using the play money as tokens. Whatever the theme, the rules stay the same: pretend money, real fun.

### Monopoly Money Amounts: Every Denomination and How Many Notes Are in the Bank
- URL: https://aupropmoney.com/blog/monopoly-money-amounts-every-denomination-and-how-many-notes-are-in-the-bank/
- Published: 2026-11-28

If you have ever opened a second-hand Monopoly box and found it short of $50 notes, you know why people search for money amounts for Monopoly. The game's money is part of the fun, and the numbers matter: how many notes are in the bank, what each denomination is for and how many of each should be in the box. This guide explains the typical denominations, how the bank works, how to count a set and how to replace missing notes with Australian play money. Editions and countries differ, so use your own rulebook as the final authority. Monopoly is a registered trademark of its owner, and PROPPS is not connected with the game.

## The short answer

A standard edition has notes from $1 to $500, a starting hand of $1,500 per player and a bank that holds the rest. If notes are missing, a small play money set in similar denominations will do. See our [Australian play money range](/shop/event-and-party-props/) for ready-made sets, and read [how much money you start with in Monopoly](/blog/how-much-money-do-you-start-with-in-the-monopoly-game-and-how-to-play-with-more/) for the starting hand.

## The usual Monopoly denominations

Standard editions use these notes:

| Denomination | Typical use |
|---|---|
| $1 | Change, small fees |
| $5 | Rent on cheap properties, change |
| $10 | Rent, small fines |
| $20 | Common payments, salary part |
| $50 | Property purchases, rent |
| $100 | Larger purchases |
| $500 | Premium purchases, big rent |

Some editions add a $200 salary note or a different mix, so check the rules. The idea is a range that lets players pay exactly and receive change.

## Counting the bank

Most boxes contain enough notes for a normal game of up to eight players. The exact number of each denomination is printed in the rules, or can be counted from a full set. If your box is second-hand, count the notes by denomination before the first game and write down what is missing. This stops arguments later.

## What each denomination is for

- $1 and $5 notes are the most important for change. If they run out, the game slows down.

- $10 and $20 notes handle most rent and fees.

- $50 and $100 notes pay for properties and houses.

- $500 notes are for the biggest deals and hotels.

Smaller notes run out first in a long game. Keep spares.

## What to do if notes are missing

There are three simple fixes.

1. IOUs. Write the amount on paper. Fast, but messy.

2. Mix in a play money set. Add a small set in the denominations you are short of, marked so you know which notes are the add-ins.

3. Swap in a full replacement set. Useful if your original is badly worn.

For a family game, a play money set in Australian-style notes is the easiest solution. The [event and party prop cash pack](/shop/event-and-party-props/event-and-party-prop-cash-pack/) has the common denominations, and the guide to [Monopoly money vs Australian play money](/blog/monopoly-money-vs-australian-play-money-what-to-use-for-board-games-and-parties/) explains how they compare.

## Printing a replacement set

A printable Monopoly money sheet can save a game night, but it is slow to cut and short-lived. See [play money printouts](/blog/play-money-printouts-australia-print-at-home-or-buy-a-ready-made-set/) for a comparison of printing and buying. Whatever you print should be clearly game money, not a copy of real currency.

## Running the bank well

A good banker keeps the bank tidy. Sort notes by denomination in a tray. Keep their own money separate. Announce every payment. Count notes into players' hands and out of the bank. These small habits prevent most arguments and make the game faster.

## Teaching with Monopoly money

Monopoly money is a useful teaching tool. Children can count by fives, add rent and calculate change. A teacher can set tasks such as making $265 using the fewest notes. Our guides to [classroom play money lessons](/blog/fake-money-for-classroom-play-money-lessons-by-year-level/) and [toy shop money games](/blog/toy-shop-money-games-play-money-for-pretend-shops-and-kids-learning/) show how.

## Keep every set clearly play money

Whether you use the original notes or a replacement set, the money should be clearly play. The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) covers counterfeit currency, and the [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions. PROPPS notes carry a clear non-legal-tender marking. Our [compliance page](/compliance/) explains the standard.

## Common mistakes

- Not counting a second-hand set. Missing notes surface mid-game.

- Running out of $1 and $5 notes. Keep spares.

- Mixing add-in notes without marking them. Keep them in a separate tray.

- Letting notes get wet. Paper curls and tears.

## How the bank is meant to work
The bank is the central store of money in the game. It pays salary when players pass Go, collects taxes and fines and sells properties. The bank is not supposed to run out of money, and in most rulebooks, if it does, the banker may issue more using paper or IOUs. A well-stocked bank keeps the game moving, which is why people want to know the right number of notes.

## Why small notes run out first
The $1 and $5 notes are used for rent and change in nearly every turn, so they run out before the larger notes do. When this happens, players hand over a large note and wait for change that the banker cannot give. Having a small play money set in $1, $5 and $10 notes solves this. If your game keeps running short of small notes, add a spare bag to the bank.

## Counting a worn set
Over time, a set loses notes. Count by denomination, compare to the rulebook and write down what is missing. If you are short only a few notes, you can use pieces of paper marked with the value as temporary notes. If you are short many, buy a replacement set. Keep a small card in the box listing the full count so you can check quickly.

## Using Australian play money as a replacement
An Australian-style play money set has notes in $5, $10, $20, $50 and $100, which cover most of the Monopoly range. You may need to treat a $100 note as a $500 note or a $5 note as a $1 note, but you should agree this at the start of the game. Mark the replacement notes with a pen or keep them in their own tray. The most important thing is that every player knows what each note is worth.

## Counting rules for large games
In games of six or more players, count the bank before play. Allow extra time for the banker to hand out starting hands. Consider appointing a second banker for the properties, so one person handles money and the other handles deeds. This keeps the game fast and avoids mistakes.

## Teaching number sense with Monopoly notes
Monopoly notes make a great maths tool. Ask children to sort the notes by value, count them in groups of five, or make a target amount with the fewest notes. For older students, ask them to work out the total in the bank. These tasks need no preparation and use materials you already have. See our guide to [classroom play money lessons](/blog/fake-money-for-classroom-play-money-lessons-by-year-level/) for more activities.

## Care and storage
Store the notes in the box with a divider for each denomination. Keep the box flat and dry. If the notes are curled, press them under a book overnight. If they are sticky or torn, replace them. A well-kept set lasts for years, and a small play money pack in the cupboard means a missing note never ends a game.

## Quick reference for game night
Keep a small card in the box with the key numbers: the starting hand for each player, the salary for passing Go, the usual denominations and any house rules you have agreed. Also note how many notes of each value are meant to be in the box, so you can check a second-hand set at a glance. Update the card when you add replacement notes. A card like this takes a few minutes to make and saves the same argument at the start of every game.

## Making your own spare bank
If your box keeps running short, assemble a spare bank in a zip bag: twenty $1 notes, twenty $5 notes, fifteen $10 notes and ten $20 notes from a play money set. Label it spare bank and keep it with the game. When the main bank runs low, tip in the spare and carry on. It is the cheapest and fastest fix for the most common problem in long games.

PROPPS orders start at the $150 AUD minimum, delivery is free from $500 AUD and cryptocurrency payments receive a 10% discount. We invoice and ship from Eltham, Melbourne by [Australia Post Express](https://auspost.com.au/) with a signature on delivery. See the [shipping policy](/shipping-policy/) for times and the [refund policy](/refund-policy/) for the 3 to 8 business day refund window.

## Fake Australian money for film sets

## A buyer's checklist for fake Australian money
Before you order, write down five answers. Who will handle the notes: actors, guests or only the camera? How close will the camera be? How many denominations does the scene need? How many resets or shoot days are planned? When must the parcel arrive? With those answers, the order almost writes itself. A camera-only shot needs a small set and careful lighting. A scene with actors needs spares because notes crease with handling. A party needs a float for every guest.

## How actors and crews handle fake Australian money
Notes survive better when the crew handles them with care. Give actors clean hands, keep stacks in a flat box between takes and use a strap for bundles so edges stay tidy. If a note gets creased, set it aside for background use and replace it in close-ups. A sensible production keeps two tiers: hero notes for the lens and working notes for everything else. This habit extends the life of every order and keeps the picture sharp.

## Lighting fake Australian money for a photo
Light decides whether notes look real. Use a large soft source from the side, add a white card opposite to fill shadows and avoid direct flash, which flattens colour and creates glare on the finish. Shoot slightly above the notes at a gentle angle so the colours and edges show. Keep the background clean and plain so the notes stand out. A few test frames before the real shoot save a lot of editing.

## Wide shots, close-ups and the money in between
Wide shots only need the colour and shape of the notes to read as cash, so stacks of lower detail work well and keep the cost down. Medium shots need correct proportions and tidy edges. Close-ups need the best notes you have, held steady and lit properly. Plan the order by shot type rather than by scene to avoid paying for detail the camera will never see.

At parties and events, treat the notes like any other prop. Brief the crowd, keep a count, collect notes at the end and store them flat. Tell venue staff what is being used so nobody is surprised. For fast-moving crowd moments such as a cash cannon finale, use notes made for parties and keep the hero notes for the photo corner. ### Money Gun Australia: How a Cash Cannon Works, What to Load It With and Party Rules
- URL: https://aupropmoney.com/blog/money-gun-australia-how-a-cash-cannon-works-and-party-rules/
- Published: 2026-11-13

A money gun, also called a cash gun or cash cannon, is the party prop everyone recognises: pull the trigger and a stream of paper notes sprays across the room. If you searched for a money gun in Australia, you probably want one for a birthday, a bucks or hens night, a reveal, a music video or a photo, and you want to know how it works, what to load into it and how to use it without trouble. This guide covers all of that in plain terms. It is general information, not legal advice. Every PROPPS product is a non-legal tender prop.

## The short answer

A money gun is a small hand-held device with a spinning wheel or roller that grabs the top note from a stack and flicks it out of the front. You load a stack of paper notes, switch it on and squeeze the trigger. The notes fly a metre or two and flutter down. Use clearly pretend play notes in it, never realistic reproductions of Australian notes, keep the area tidy, and photograph it so nobody could mistake the notes for real money. The [Party Cash Cannon Kit](/shop/event-and-party-props/party-cash-cannon-kit/) is built around exactly that rule.

## How a money gun works

Most cash cannons use a small motor, a rubber wheel and a spring-loaded tray. The tray presses the stack against the wheel, the wheel spins when you pull the trigger and each turn pushes one note through a slot at the front. A few simple toy models work by hand with a lever. The notes need to be thin, flat and about the right size, which is why the better kits ship with their own purpose-made paper notes rather than relying on whatever paper you have.

Because the notes feed one at a time, a jam is the usual fault. Creased, damp or stuck-together notes are the main cause. Fan the stack before loading, keep the notes dry and load only what the tray is designed to hold.

## What to load into a money gun

This is the question that matters most. A money gun scatters notes through a crowd, and in a crowd notes end up in pockets, handbags, gutters and car parks. That is why the notes in the gun should be clearly pretend.

- Party play notes, printed PLAY MONEY. Bright, obviously unlike real currency and not a copy of an Australian note. These are the notes to fire.

- Realistic prop notes. Do not fire them. A realistic reproduction that leaves the venue can be mistaken for real money, even with a specimen marking. Our guide to [novelty money for parties and events](/blog/novelty-money-for-parties-and-events-whats-legal-in-australia/) makes the same point.

- Real money. Never. It is not a prop and you will lose it.

The kit includes the play notes for the cannon and one separate stack of specimen-marked PROPPS notes for the photo or video. The stack stays with the host and is never loaded or fired.

## Where the law comes in

The Commonwealth Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 is aimed at counterfeit currency and reproductions that could deceive a reasonable person. The [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions, and you can read the Act at [legislation.gov.au](https://www.legislation.gov.au/). In broad terms, clearly marked props used as props are treated very differently from notes made to pass as real. Firing obviously pretend play notes sits at the safe end of that range. Read our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and the [compliance page](/compliance/) for how PROPPS builds to the standard.

## Safety and where to use it

A money gun is a toy for adults and older children, so treat it like any party device. Keep it away from faces, particularly eyes, and do not point it at people at close range. Check the manufacturer's age guidance, and see the [Product Safety Australia](https://www.productsafety.gov.au/) site if you are buying for children. Use it indoors on a floor you can sweep or outdoors where the notes will not blow onto a road. Keep batteries, if the model uses them, away from small children, and remove them when you store it.

## Money gun at a party: simple rules

1. Choose one person to run the cannon. They load it and control who fires.

2. Brief the crowd. Tell guests the notes are party props and should be left on the floor, not taken home or used as payment.

3. Brief the venue and staff. Bar and door staff should know what is being fired.

4. Collect and count. Sweep the notes up at the end. Bag the play notes and bin or reuse them, and count the marked stack back in.

5. Do not use the notes as payment, even as a joke. Never.

## Money gun for photos and video

A money gun looks great on camera, and it also makes it easy to post a picture that gets misread. A clear photo of someone holding a fan of realistic notes with a caption about winning or gifting cash is the kind of post that attracts complaints. Make it obvious the money is a prop. Fire the play notes for the action shot, and use the separate marked stack in a still set-up with the gun beside it. Our [guide for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/) explains how to present prop money honestly, and the guide to [lighting prop money for camera](/blog/lighting-prop-money-for-camera-avoiding-glare/) helps with glare.

## What the best money gun kit includes

Searches for the best money gun usually come down to a few things: a sturdy body, reliable feeding, notes made for the machine and a clear way to keep the setup safe and legal. When you compare a cash cannon, check these points.

- The notes. Purpose-made play notes feed better than office paper and look obviously pretend.

- Power. Check whether it runs on batteries or a cable, and what is included.

- Build. A solid housing and a decent trigger last through a whole party, not just the first song.

- The photo prop. A clearly marked stack for the picture, kept separate from the notes you fire.

- Paperwork. An Australian supplier who invoices and ships with tracking.

## Planning how many notes you need

A cash cannon fires notes quickly. A hundred notes can be gone in under half a minute, so plan the moment. For a reveal or a first-dance finale, a single load is plenty. For a longer party, keep a spare pack and a helper to reload. If you want to run a casino night or game stall as well, use [play money for events](/shop/event-and-party-props/) for the tables, kept separate from the cannon's notes.

## Money gun, confetti cannon or something else?

A confetti cannon is a different product, a single burst of paper or foil. A money gun is a repeat fire device with a money theme, and it needs the safety rules above. If you only want a one-off burst, a confetti cannon is simpler. If the money theme is the point, whether for a themed night, a music video or a surprise, the cash cannon is the better pick.

## Cleaning up and keeping the venue happy

Venues care about two things: mess and surprises. Tell the venue manager before the event that you will be using a cash cannon with paper play notes, ask where the cleaning gear is and agree who sweeps up. Paper notes are light, so a small hand broom and a bag clear a dance floor in minutes. Outdoors, watch the wind, because notes travel further than you expect, and never fire near a pool, a road or a car park. A quick heads-up and a tidy finish keep the venue happy and make it easier to book again.

## Five quick party plans

Birthday finale. Load the play notes, count down, fire. Sweep the notes the next morning.

Bucks or hens night. One person runs the cannon, and the marked stack sits on the table for photos.

Reveal or announcement. One load, one fire and a clear caption on the photo that it is party money.

Music video or social shoot. Fire play notes for movement, shoot the stack separately and add a caption that the money is a prop.

Corporate night. Use it as a prize moment, with a briefing and a collect-and-count at the end.

## After the party

Sweep up every note you can find. Bag the play notes and reuse them for the next event or discard them. Keep the marked stack with the invoice and store it flat and dry. Remove the batteries from the cannon if you are putting it away for a while.

## Common mistakes

- Loading realistic notes. They will leave the venue.

- Letting guests take marked notes home. One note in a wallet can turn into a question later.

- Skipping the briefing. Staff and guests should know it is a prop.

- Overloading the tray. It jams and the party stalls.

- Posting a photo without context. Add a line that the money is a prop.

### Prop Dollar vs Prop Cash vs Prop Money: What Each Term Means in Australia
- URL: https://aupropmoney.com/blog/prop-dollar-vs-prop-cash-vs-prop-money/
- Published: 2026-10-26

If you are searching for a prop dollar, prop cash or prop money, you could be looking for three different things. A prop dollar is one note. Prop cash is the loose, handled look of money on screen. Prop money is the product category that covers both. Getting the terms straight saves you from ordering the wrong quantity, the wrong finish or the wrong denomination, and it helps an insurer or production manager read your brief the same way you do.

This guide sets out what each term means for Australian film, television, theatre and photography work, how the three differ in practice, and how to turn the words into an order. It is general information about props, not legal advice.

## Quick answer: how the three terms differ

- Prop dollar: a single reproduction note, usually described by its denomination, for example a $50 prop dollar. It is what you hold in a close-up.
- Prop cash: money as it reads in a scene, meaning bundles, rolls, fanned notes and loose handfuls that look used rather than fresh from the printer.
- Prop money: the umbrella term for every non-legal tender reproduction note made for productions, from one note to a pallet.

In practice a prop dollar is the unit, prop cash is the look and prop money is the product. Most orders mix all three: a few hero notes for the close-up and enough stacks to fill the frame.

## What is a prop dollar?

A prop dollar is one reproduction banknote. On a call sheet it appears as "hero note", "insert note" or by denomination. The hero note is the one the camera sees, so it gets the most attention: crisp printing, even colour and clear specimen markings. Australia's notes are polymer, and our reproductions are paper-based, which is one of the deliberate differences that keeps them clearly distinct from genuine currency.

If you need a close-up of a single note, start with the denomination pages: the [$5](/shop/new-notes/5-australian-prop-money-for-sale/), [$10](/shop/new-notes/10-australian-prop-money-for-sale/), [$20](/shop/new-notes/20-australian-prop-money-for-sale/), [$50](/shop/new-notes/50-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) and [$100](/shop/new-notes/100-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) products each carry the specimen markings required by our standard.

## What is prop cash?

Prop cash is the on-screen impression of money. A single crisp note says "new". A handful of slightly bent notes in a coat pocket says "this has been spent". Art departments talk about prop cash when they plan texture, wear and volume rather than a single note. That is why the [art department guide to weathering prop cash](/blog/art-department-guide-weathering-prop-cash/) matters: the same stack looks different depending on how it has been handled.

Prop cash is usually bought in stacks. A [money stack](/shop/money-stacks/) is a bundled quantity of one denomination or a mix, strapped the way a bank would strap them, so it reads as a real sum even at a distance. If you are planning how many you need, our guide on [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) gives a counting method by shot type.

## What is prop money?

Prop money is the broad category: reproduction notes sold for motion pictures, television, theatre, photography and training. When someone asks "can I buy prop money in Australia", they mean the whole category, and the answer is yes when the notes are clearly marked and not used to deceive. Our post on [whether you can buy prop money in Australia](/blog/can-you-buy-prop-money-in-australia/) walks through it, and the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) is where the marked reproductions live.

## Side by side

| Term | What it is | Typical quantity | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prop dollar | One reproduction note | 1 to 20 | Close-ups, inserts, hero notes |
| Prop cash | The handled, lived-in look | Loose notes to small stacks | Pockets, wallets, tables, bar tops |
| Prop money | The full category | Any | Briefing, budgeting and ordering |

## Which one do you actually need?

Match the term to the shot rather than the other way round.

1. Close-up of a single note. You need a prop dollar in the right denomination. Check the artwork at the size the camera will see it.
2. A hand counting notes. You need prop cash: a stack of the same denomination, lightly aged, with the strap on.
3. A suitcase or table of money. You need prop money in volume. Buy more than you think, because notes get damaged and reshoots happen.
4. A party or classroom. You probably want play money, not specimen reproductions. Read [play money vs prop money](/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/) first.

## How the terms show up on a prop schedule

Art departments rarely write "prop cash" on a schedule without a number beside it. A tidy prop line reads like "Scene 14, bank counter, 3 x strapped stacks of $100 prop dollars, 6 loose hero notes". That one line carries all three ideas: the denomination (the prop dollar), the volume (the stacks) and the finish (the loose hero notes that have been handled). Writing it this way makes ordering quick, because your supplier can read the quantities straight off the line.

A useful habit is to give every money line three details: the denomination, the count and the condition. Denomination tells you which product page to start from. Count tells you whether you need a single note, a stack or a bulk pack. Condition tells you whether to request notes that look fresh, lightly handled or heavily worn.

## Common mix-ups to avoid

- Ordering one note when you meant a stack. "A prop dollar" is one note. If the script says "a wad of cash", you need a strapped stack.
- Treating "prop cash" as a different product. It is the same reproduction notes, styled and aged. You do not need a separate supplier for it.
- Using "prop money" to mean play money. The two are made for different jobs. Play money is a toy, while prop money is a film-grade reproduction. Check which one your brief needs.
- Mixing denominations without a reason. A real till holds a mix, but a bank-vault shot usually uses one denomination per strap. Decide the look first.
- Forgetting the marking. Whatever you call the notes, they must carry a clear specimen marking.

## Examples by production type

Short film or student project. A handful of prop dollars for insert shots, plus one or two stacks. Orders start at $150 AUD, so most small shoots buy a mixed stack and use it across scenes.

Television drama. Prop cash in volume: stacks of $50 and $100 for deals and payoffs, with a few hero notes. Series work often reorders for each block, so keep the supplier invoice and the count from the last order.

Theatre. Prop dollars used as stage cash, usually in a prop wallet or bundle. The audience is further away, so denomination colour matters more than fine print detail.

Photography and content. A fan of prop dollars or a stack on a table. The shot is often a close-up, so check the print quality, and read our guide to [prop money for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/) before you publish.

## What stays the same whichever word you use

Whatever you call it, the legal position does not change. A reproduction must be clearly distinguishable from a genuine note, marked, and used only as a prop. The Reserve Bank publishes its [banknote reproduction guidance](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/), and the offences sit in the Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/). Our [compliance page](/compliance/) explains the specimen markings on every PROPPS note, and the longer guide to the [Crimes (Currency) Act and RBA rules](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) covers the detail.

Three habits keep any prop dollar or stack of prop cash on the right side of the line:

- Keep notes with the art department, not in a wallet.
- Never spend them, hand them over or post them as if they were real cash.
- Keep the supplier invoice on the production file.

## How to order

Pick the denominations for your close-ups first, then add stacks for the volume. Orders start at $150 AUD, delivery is free from $500 AUD, and payments in cryptocurrency receive a 10% discount. Parcels leave our Eltham, Melbourne depot by Australia Post Express with a mandatory signature, usually within 24 business hours of payment. For studio-scale quantities, ask about the [wholesale tiers](/wholesale/) of 10% to 30% off.
